Command turns a request into an object instead of a function call made and forgotten. The class implements at least
; each instance stores exactly the arguments one particular call needed, so that calling
later needs nothing else, and calling
can reverse exactly that call rather than guess at a new one. The object making the request builds a
and hands it to whatever will run it; that receiver does not need to know what the command does, only that it can be executed.

The problem is a call that has to happen somewhere other than where it was decided: queued for later, run on a different thread, written to a log, sent across a network, or reversed. A function call is gone the instant it returns; nothing about it can be replayed, inspected first, or undone, because there was never an object to hold and look at.
The mechanism is packaging a request as data before it runs: the receiver and the arguments become member variables,
performs the call using them, and
, when the command supports it, performs the inverse using the same stored data. A queue is

waiting to be executed; a history is the same commands moved into a second list after they run, ready to be undone in reverse order; a macro command holds a list of other commands and executes or undoes all of them as one.

What it costs is an object and a virtual call where a direct call would have done, and a class per kind of request. Skip it for a call that runs once, right where it is made, and never needs to be queued, logged or undone: that call is smaller and clearer written directly. Reach for it once any of those four needs shows up, because retrofitting undo into code that only ever called functions means finding every call site and deciding what its inverse is, after the fact.
You meet this in any editor, planner or console with an undo command, and the interview question is exactly the shape that makes undo possible: an object that remembers enough to reverse itself.
